title: Egress flow control heuristics and measurement
body:
Purpose and motivation:

This is a working notes doc capturing the heuristic designs and measurement results from our April experiments that probe egress-side flow control across HTTP/1.1, HTTP/2, and gRPC streaming paths when there is a mixed workload of short-turn chat and long-running streaming responses. The goal: derive a small set of deployable heuristics for (1) edge proxy pacing, (2) per-connection token-bucket tuning, and (3) adaptive fanout limits for multiplexer proxies that yield better p50/p95 latency without blowing throughput.

Background / problem statement:
- We observed widened tail latencies under mixed workloads where a handful of long streaming responses would slow delivery for many short requests. Suspected causes: TCP head-of-line effects at the proxy, TLS record sizing, application-level chunking policies, and token-bucket misconfiguration in the egress stack.
- Existing mitigation experiments (simple per-connection queues, fixed small chunk sizes) moved the needle but had tradeoffs: higher overall CPU and increased token usage. Need a reproducible measurement framework and an actionable heuristics set.

Experiment matrix (overview):
- Testbed: 3-node cluster (1 ingress proxy, 1 serving runtime node, 1 client generator) on c5/rtx-like instances within same AZ. All traffic TLS.
- Workloads: 
  * bursty short requests: 30k requests over 60s; mean payload 200 tokens; target 50 ms server compute.
  * long streams: 300 concurrent streams emitting 1 token/sec for 120s (simulates streaming chat with live typing).
  * mix ratios: 80/20, 50/50, 20/80 short/long.
- Protocols: HTTP/1.1 chunked, HTTP/2 multiplexed, gRPC bidi streaming.
- Proxy variants: Envoy baseline, Envoy + egress pacing filter (our prototype), small custom uproxy with per-connection NB token bucket.
- Measured metrics: client-observed p50/p95/p99 latency for short requests, server CPU, proxy egress queue length, TLS record size distribution, per-connection bytes-in-flight, observed retransmits (via tcpdump), and application-level stall times (time between token sends for a stream).

Key results (short summary):
- HTTP/1.1 chunking with fixed 1KB chunk size gave best p50 but poor p95 when long streams saturated link (head-of-line blocking from long-lived connection writes).
- HTTP/2 multiplexing reduced head-of-line at TCP level, but with default WINDOW_UPDATE behavior we saw stalls in application scheduling causing bursts when windows were updated (p95 worse than expected).
- gRPC bidi streams behaved like HTTP/2 with added complexity: many small messages caused CPU overhead in framing and context switches on the proxy.
- Our egress pacing filter that enforces a light-weight per-connection pacing (packet pacing + application chunk delay) reduced p95 short-request latency by 30–45% at the cost of ~8% extra CPU on the proxy node.
- Adaptive fanout limit (max concurrent outstanding messages per upstream connection) prevented tail amplification: applying a soft-limit of 8 concurrent outstanding messages per connection reduced p99 by ~60% in 50/50 mixes.

Detailed findings and evidence:
1) TLS record size and small-write amplification:
- Observation: many small application writes (single-token writes) created many 1–200 byte TLS records. This increased CPU and caused bursts at network egress.
- Measurement: we collected TLS record size histogram with tshark; >65% of records were <256 bytes under naive writing.
- Suggestion: coalesce small application writes into 512–1k records at the proxy when latency budget permits. Add a small 1–2ms batching window for short requests only.

2) Token-bucket placement matters:
- We tried token buckets at: a) per-proxy global egress, b) per-connection, c) per-stream (gRPC).
- Per-connection buckets best balanced fairness and simplicity. Per-stream had excessive state and context switch overhead; global buckets starved small flows when long flows grabbed capacity.

3) Multiplexing window_update scheduling:
- HTTP/2 default window updates can create microbursts. Our tracing showed application threads would schedule writes in bursts after window update callbacks.
- Heuristic: stagger window updates by random jitter (0–2ms) when updating many streams at once. Implemented as a patch to our HTTP/2 shim in the proxy; p95 improved ~15% in tests.

4) Adaptive fanout / outstanding message cap:
- Root cause for tail amplification: a proxy will forward many upstream messages concurrently; if upstream network stalls, the write queue grows and prevents short messages from being flushed.
- Heuristic: hard cap concurrent outstanding messages per upstream connection (8) with a small per-connection fair queue for new short requests. When cap reached, short requests are queued and given higher priority on release. This reduces head-of-line for short requests.

Implementation notes (prototype configs):
- Egress pacing filter options tested:
  pacing.enabled = true
  pacing.min_chunk_bytes = 512
  pacing.max_chunk_bytes = 1024
  pacing.batching_ms = 1-3  # dynamic based on RTT
  pacing.cpu_budget_pct = 10
- Per-connection token bucket: 
  tokens_per_sec = 1_000_000 (bytes)
  burst_bytes = 32_768
  slow_start_window = 100ms

Commands & reproducibility notes:
- client generator used: wrk2 with custom script for streaming; we also used a small go-based harness (repo link in linked_artifacts) that opens gRPC bidi streams and emits token-sized messages on schedule.
- packet capture: tcpdump -i eth0 -w egress-mix-50-50.pcap host <proxy-ip>
- TLS sizes: tshark -r egress-mix-50-50.pcap -Y "ssl.record.length" -T fields -e ssl.record.length | awk '{print $1}' | ./histogram.py

Open questions / tradeoffs:
- How aggressive can batching be for short requests before we start to harm p50? Early tests show 1–2ms batching window is a sweet spot, but may vary by region/RTO. Need cross-region tests.
- CPU vs latency trade: pacing reduces tail but increases CPU. Where to surface this in autoscaling? Candidate: a blue/green rollout that ties pacing CPU budget to an autoscaler label.
- gRPC message coalescing: library-level coalescing could help, but it requires changes in client lib and risk violating low-latency streaming semantics. Prefer proxy-level coalescing in the short term.

Action items / next experiments:
- Run 3-region sweep to validate batching window sensitivity (assigned: Evan). Due: 2026-04-22.
- Integrate the egress pacing filter into our Envoy fork as an opt-in feature flag and run a canary on non-customer-critical cluster (assigned: Sofia). Due: 2026-04-28.
- Add per-connection outstanding-message metric to our tracing and export as a sampling counter in the proxy (assigned: Aisha). Due: 2026-04-20.

Notes to self / rough TODOs:
- Add screenshots of TLS histograms and p95 curves to a follow-up doc (will export graphs from bench infra).
- Draft a short one-pager for product to explain tradeoffs (latency vs cost) for Dedicated customers.

Signals to watch if we enable heuristics in production:
- p50/p95 short-request latency, proxy CPU, per-connection bytes-in-flight, error rates (especially 13/RESOURCE_EXHAUSTED on gRPC), and billing token consumption (to ensure no unexpected cost increase).

References / links:
- Linked PR with prototype filter: https://github.com/redwood-inference/serving-runtime/pull/482
- Linear ticket for follow-up automation: https://linear.app/redwood/issue/NET-447/egress-throttling-experiment

End of notes.
